items.stem: Why is the open ocean often described as a "marine desert"?
items.answer: Nutrients are scarce in the sunlit surface layer
items.markingKey: Nutrients are scarce in the sunlit surface layer. Nutrients sink below the photic zone.

items.stem: Compare freshwater ecosystems with marine ecosystems.
items.answer: Freshwater ecosystems (lakes, rivers, wetlands) have low salinity and are small and often nutrient-rich; marine ecosystems are saline, cover about 71% of Earth's surface and are mostly nutrient-poor except on shelves and in upwellings.
items.markingKey: Freshwater ecosystems (lakes, rivers, wetlands) have low salinity and are small and often nutrient-rich; marine ecosystems are saline, cover about 71% of Earth's surface and are mostly nutrient-poor except on shelves and in upwellings. items.stem: Explain the difference between capture fisheries and aquaculture.
items.answer: Capture fisheries harvest wild stocks; aquaculture farms aquatic organisms in controlled conditions (cages, ponds, rafts).
items.markingKey: Capture fisheries harvest wild stocks; aquaculture farms aquatic organisms in controlled conditions (cages, ponds, rafts). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why harvesting at lower trophic levels is more efficient.
items.answer: Less energy has been lost through respiration in earlier transfers, so more biomass is available per unit of primary production; e.g. farming seaweed or mussels rather than tuna.

items.stem: Sofia writes: "The open ocean is the most productive marine ecosystem per square metre." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The open ocean has very low productivity per m² because surface nutrients are scarce; it is large in total only because of its area.
items.markingKey: The open ocean has very low productivity per m² because surface nutrients are scarce; it is large in total only because of its area. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why mangrove forests are important to coastal fisheries.
items.answer: They act as nurseries for juvenile fish and shrimp, provide shelter and food from leaf litter, filter sediments and protect coasts.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Grand Banks cod collapse and explain what it reveals about the consequences of fishing beyond MSY.
items.answer: Catches peaked at about 800,000 t in 1968; by 1992 the spawning stock had fallen by over 95%, and a moratorium closed the fishery. Overfishing removed the breeding stock, and the ecosystem shifted (more shrimp and crab), so recovery has been very slow.

items.stem: A Schaefer surplus-production model for Atlantic cod on the Grand Banks gives intrinsic growth rate r = 0.4 per year and carrying capacity K = 1,500 thousand tonnes; surplus yield Y = rN(1 − N/K). The stock is currently estimated at 1050 thousand tonnes. (a) Calculate the MSY and the current surplus yield. (b) A fishing industry body proposes a quota of 187.5 thousand tonnes per year. Explain the likely consequence for the stock. (c) Evaluate the use of MSY as the basis of fisheries management, with reference to a named fishery.
items.answer: (a) MSY = 150 thousand tonnes per year at N = 750; current Y = 0.4 × 1050 × (1 − 1050/1500) = 126.0 thousand tonnes per year (b) the quota exceeds both MSY and current surplus production, so the catch removes more than natural increase; the stock will decline, reducing future yields and risking collapse (as with Grand Banks cod, 1992). (c) MSY gives a clear, science-based target, but r and K are uncertain and change with environment; it ignores age structure, bycatch and ecosystem interactions; variable recruitment and political pressure lead to quotas above advice; precautionary targets (e.g. F below F_MSY, ecosystem-based management) are safer.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 150, M1 substitution, A1 126.0. (b) R1 harvest > surplus → decline, R1 named consequence. (c) R1 strength, R1 limitation with example.

items.stem: With reference to shrimp farming in Thailand, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in the environmental costs of aquaculture. [7]
items.answer: From the 1980s large areas of mangrove were cleared for shrimp ponds, many of which were abandoned after a few years because of disease and pollution. Intensive ponds destroyed coastal protection and nursery habitats, leaving degraded land when disease forced abandonment. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: A Schaefer surplus-production model for southern bluefin tuna gives intrinsic growth rate r = 0.4 per year and carrying capacity K = 600 thousand tonnes; surplus yield Y = rN(1 − N/K). The stock is currently estimated at 420 thousand tonnes. (a) Calculate the MSY and the current surplus yield. (b) A fishing industry body proposes a quota of 84 thousand tonnes per year. Explain the likely consequence for the stock. (c) Evaluate the use of MSY as the basis of fisheries management, with reference to a named fishery.
items.answer: (a) MSY = 60 thousand tonnes per year at N = 300; current Y = 0.4 × 420 × (1 − 420/600) = 50.4 thousand tonnes per year (b) the quota exceeds both MSY and current surplus production, so the catch removes more than natural increase; the stock will decline, reducing future yields and risking collapse (as with Grand Banks cod, 1992). (c) MSY gives a clear, science-based target, but r and K are uncertain and change with environment; it ignores age structure, bycatch and ecosystem interactions; variable recruitment and political pressure lead to quotas above advice; precautionary targets (e.g. F below F_MSY, ecosystem-based management) are safer.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 60, M1 substitution, A1 50.4. (b) R1 harvest > surplus → decline, R1 named consequence. (c) R1 strength, R1 limitation with example.

items.stem: Using the Tonlé Sap lake, Cambodia as an example, explain freshwater ecosystem productivity.
items.answer: The Mekong reverses flow in the wet season, expanding the lake about five-fold and supporting a fish catch of several hundred thousand tonnes a year. The seasonal flood pulse brings nutrients and floods forests that act as spawning and feeding grounds.
items.markingKey: Context (The Mekong reverses flow in the wet season, expanding the lake about five-fold and supporting a fish catch of several hundred thousand tonnes a year.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The seasonal flood pulse brings nutrients and floods forests that act as spawning and feeding grounds. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to freshwater ecosystem productivity.

items.stem:
The following information comes from a case study.

Feed conversion ratios (kg feed per kg live-weight gain, approximate): farmed salmon 1.2-1.4; tilapia 1.5-1.8; chicken 1.7-2.0; pork 2.7-3.0; beef 6-10; mussels 0 (no added feed).

Explain why fish generally have lower FCRs than land livestock.
items.answer: Fish are ectotherms, so less energy is used maintaining body temperature; water supports their body so less energy is spent on skeleton and movement.
items.markingKey: Fish are ectotherms, so less energy is used maintaining body temperature; water supports their body so less energy is spent on skeleton and movement. Award [1] per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; quoted data must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Northern cod (Grand Banks) landings (thousand tonnes, approximate): 1960 - 450; 1968 - 810; 1975 - 290; 1985 - 230; 1991 - 190; 1993 - 10 (moratorium from 1992).

Explain why the stock had not recovered by the 2010s despite the moratorium.
items.answer: The breeding stock was too small; cod mature slowly (6-7 years); ecosystem changes (more predators such as seals, changes in prey such as capelin); some bycatch and recreational fishing continued.
items.markingKey: The breeding stock was too small; cod mature slowly (6-7 years); ecosystem changes (more predators such as seals, changes in prey such as capelin); some bycatch and recreational fishing continued. items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that freshwater fisheries deserve as much protection as marine fisheries.
items.answer: Freshwater fisheries deserve equal or greater protection because of their importance to the poorest communities and steep biodiversity decline.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: support food security for millions inland (Mekong, Lake Victoria); freshwater biodiversity declining fastest (85% LPI). Limitations / counter-points: smaller total catch; marine stocks have larger global economic value. Conclusion: Freshwater fisheries deserve equal or greater protection because of their importance to the poorest communities and steep biodiversity decline. items.stem: To what extent do you agree that aquaculture is the solution to declining wild fish stocks? [9]
items.answer: Aquaculture can relieve pressure on wild stocks if it focuses on low-trophic species and sustainable feed, but it is not a solution on its own.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: already supplies over half of aquatic animal food; efficient conversion (FCR 1-2); low-trophic species need no feed. items.stem: Define the term "marine protected area (MPA)".
items.answer: An area of sea where human activities such as fishing are restricted to protect ecosystems
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an area of sea where human activities such as fishing are restricted to protect ecosystems. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "continental shelf"?
options: The shallow, gently sloping seabed around continents (usually < 200 m deep) where light and nutrients support high productivity and most fisheries
A share of a TAC allocated to a fisher or company that can be bought, sold or leased
Non-target species (dolphins, turtles, juvenile fish) caught unintentionally during fishing
The upper layer of a water body where there is enough light for photosynthesis, usually down to about 200 m
items.answer: The shallow, gently sloping seabed around continents (usually < 200 m deep) where light and nutrients support high productivity and most fisheries
items.markingKey: A. "continental shelf" is the shallow, gently sloping seabed around continents (usually < 200 m deep) where light and nutrients support high productivity and most fisheries.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The mass of feed needed to produce a unit increase in body mass of a farmed animal"?
items.answer: feed conversion ratio (FCR)
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of feed conversion ratio (FCR).

items.stem: Outline why setting quotas at MSY can still lead to overfishing.
items.answer: MSY depends on uncertain estimates of r and K; environmental variation changes recruitment; illegal and unreported catches and discards increase actual mortality; MSY ignores bycatch and ecosystem effects.
items.markingKey: MSY depends on uncertain estimates of r and K; environmental variation changes recruitment; illegal and unreported catches and discards increase actual mortality; MSY ignores bycatch and ecosystem effects. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: "Fish are only an important food in coastal countries." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Freshwater fisheries (e.g. Mekong, Lake Victoria, Tonlé Sap) supply protein to many inland communities.
items.markingKey: Freshwater fisheries (e.g. Mekong, Lake Victoria, Tonlé Sap) supply protein to many inland communities. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between extensive aquaculture and intensive aquaculture.
items.answer: Extensive aquaculture uses natural food and low stocking densities with little input (e.g. traditional carp ponds); intensive aquaculture uses high densities, formulated feeds, aeration and medicines to maximise yield.
items.markingKey: Extensive aquaculture uses natural food and low stocking densities with little input (e.g. traditional carp ponds); intensive aquaculture uses high densities, formulated feeds, aeration and medicines to maximise yield. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline how no-take marine reserves can increase catches nearby.
items.answer: Protected fish grow larger and produce many more eggs and larvae; adults and larvae spill over into fished areas, increasing catches around the reserve (e.g. Apo Island, Philippines).
items.markingKey: Protected fish grow larger and produce many more eggs and larvae; adults and larvae spill over into fished areas, increasing catches around the reserve (e.g. Apo Island, Philippines). [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Distinguish between marine ecosystems and freshwater ecosystems.
items.answer: Freshwater ecosystems (lakes, rivers, wetlands) have low salinity and are small and often nutrient-rich; marine ecosystems are saline, cover about 71% of Earth's surface and are mostly nutrient-poor except on shelves and in upwellings.
items.markingKey: Freshwater ecosystems (lakes, rivers, wetlands) have low salinity and are small and often nutrient-rich; marine ecosystems are saline, cover about 71% of Earth's surface and are mostly nutrient-poor except on shelves and in upwellings. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Aquaculture always reduces pressure on wild fish." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Farming carnivorous species can increase demand for wild forage fish; escapes and disease can harm wild populations.
items.markingKey: Farming carnivorous species can increase demand for wild forage fish; escapes and disease can harm wild populations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using the Patagonian toothfish fishery as an example, explain international cooperation in fisheries management.
items.answer: Heavy illegal fishing in the 1990s was reduced through CCAMLR catch documentation and the MSC certification of some fisheries. Traceability and certification made illegal catch harder to sell, supporting stock recovery.
items.markingKey: Context (Heavy illegal fishing in the 1990s was reduced through CCAMLR catch documentation and the MSC certification of some fisheries.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to seaweed and shellfish farming in Sanggou Bay, China, explain how it illustrates integrated multi-trophic aquaculture.
items.answer: Integrated culture of kelp, scallops, oysters and fish produces large yields while seaweed absorbs nutrients. Combining trophic levels recycles waste nutrients into marketable products and limits eutrophication.
items.markingKey: Context (Integrated culture of kelp, scallops, oysters and fish produces large yields while seaweed absorbs nutrients.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Suggest why the Mekong River fishery is important for food security in Cambodia.
items.answer: The Tonlé Sap flood pulse supports one of the world's largest inland fisheries; fish provide most of the animal protein consumed by Cambodians; dams upstream threaten migration and sediment.
items.markingKey: The Tonlé Sap flood pulse supports one of the world's largest inland fisheries; fish provide most of the animal protein consumed by Cambodians; dams upstream threaten migration and sediment.

items.stem: With reference to salmon farming in Norway, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in impacts of intensive mariculture. [7]
items.answer: Norway produces about 1.5 million t of farmed salmon a year; sea lice are linked to declines of wild salmon in some fjords. High densities of farmed fish amplify parasites that spread to wild fish migrating past the cages. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: Suggest four measures that could help a depleted fish stock recover.
items.answer: Reduce TAC below MSY; larger mesh sizes to let juveniles escape; seasonal closures during spawning; no-take MPAs; reduce subsidies and fleet capacity; monitor catches (observers, vessel tracking); bycatch-reduction devices.
